artboards.title: Today — People on a phone: nothing tells a phone anything
A — On this phone's own row, on each house's People
B — Once, in Houses, for every house
C — Asked the first time something needs you

annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS

Today the house only speaks to whoever is looking at a screen. A phone at the door, a light that stopped answering, an account signed out: all of it waits in the band until somebody happens to open the house (docs/messages.md).

Decided already, and not what these boards are about: a phone has one notification key for every house it has joined, as the printer app does it; each house decides what is worth telling which phone; only the classes the catalog marks attention (and later alert, the household's own list) are ever sent; the store app's come through Elyir's sealed sender; and Apple or Google see that a house sent something, and when, never what (docs/apps.md, Decided).

What these boards decide is where a person says yes. Two things have to happen somewhere: the phone has to allow notifications at all, which iOS only asks inside a tap in the app itself, and each house has to know this phone wants to hear from it.

TODAY

The shipped People sheet at 390x844 on the mock house with a passcode set. Phones are listed with when they joined and when they were last seen, and can be removed. Nothing anywhere says a phone can be told anything, because none can.

A — ON THIS PHONE'S OWN ROW

On each house's People, the row for the phone you are holding grows one line: Tell this phone when something needs you, with the panel's own switch and two examples under it. Other phones' rows say what they are told, read only: only a phone can turn itself on. The first switch on a phone also asks the phone to allow notifications.

FOR: it lives where the phone already lives in the house, next to Remove, and Remove taking the notifications with it reads naturally. Each house is decided where that house is.

AGAINST: a phone with three houses says yes three times, in three places. And the tap happens inside the house's own panel, framed by the Houses app, which is not the page iOS lets ask; in the store app that is fine, and in Houses on the Home Screen it has to be proved it can work before this is chosen.

B — ONCE, IN HOUSES

The Houses sheet, under the list of houses, gets a part for the phone itself: Notifications, one switch, and a line saying each house decides what it tells you and what Apple sees. Switched on, every house this phone has joined can tell it what needs it; each house's People then shows which phones it tells, read only, the way A's other rows do.

FOR: one yes, for every house, in the one place that is the phone's own rather than any house's. The tap is in the Houses app, the page iOS lets ask, in the browser and the store app alike. Says the privacy sentence where the decision is made.

AGAINST: it is a setting, found only by somebody who goes looking in Houses, which most people never open with one house. Turning one house off needs a second level (a switch per house under it), not drawn.

C — WHEN IT FIRST MATTERS

Nothing to set up front. The first time something that needs you reaches the band on this phone (here, an iPad asking to join), the chip carries one more line: Tell this phone next time? Yes, and the phone is asked to allow notifications and this house will tell it; No, and it is not asked again by that house. Changing it later is on the phone's own row, as A draws it.

FOR: asked at the one moment the answer is obvious, which is also what Apple's own guidance asks for. Nobody meets a setting before they know why they would want it.

AGAINST: the first thing that needs you is the one thing never told to you. Like A, the tap is inside the house's panel; and C still needs A's row to change its mind, so it is A plus a moment, not instead of it.
